title: Weekly Medicaid, Home Health & HCBS Update
overviewHtml: This week's dominant theme is enforcement and effective dates catching up to policies enacted months ago, rather than new federal rate action: on October 1, CMS's noncitizen Medicaid/CHIP funding restriction took effect, Mississippi began auto-suspending Electronic Visit Verification (EVV) non-compliant personal care and private duty nursing claims, and Kansas launched its new Community Supports Waiver, while a federal court in Texas v. Kennedy vacated the community-integration provisions of HHS's Section 504 rule. I want to be explicit about what did NOT happen this week: there was no new federal Medicare home health rate cut or increase — the CY2027 Home Health Prospective Payment System rule remains a proposal with its comment period closed and no final rule issued; and there was no Medicaid funding disruption from a federal government shutdown, since Congress funded the government through December 11, 2026 back in early September. Readers should not treat any of this week's items as changing current reimbursement rates for home health, personal care, or HCBS providers generally.

items.headline: CMS Noncitizen Medicaid/CHIP Funding Restriction Takes Effect
items.status: Implemented October 1, 2026, per CMS State Health Official letter SHO #26-001.
items.bodyHtml:
Effective October 1, 2026, CMS guidance implementing Section 71109 of the 2025 federal reconciliation law limits federal Medicaid and CHIP matching funds to a narrower set of noncitizen categories — lawful permanent residents, Cuban/Haitian entrants, and residents of the Compact of Free Association (COFA) nations. Refugees, asylees, trafficking and domestic-violence survivors, and humanitarian parolees, who previously qualified for full-scope coverage, generally lose federal matching eligibility, though coverage for emergency medical conditions continues and states retain the option to cover lawfully residing children and pregnant women using state-only or other funds.

CMS's State Health Official letter (SHO #26-001) directs states on eligibility system updates, redetermination processes, verification, and claims handling needed to implement the restriction. States including Washington have already begun processing coverage terminations tied to this change effective October 1.

The Congressional Budget Office has estimated the Medicaid/CHIP-specific eligibility restrictions will increase the uninsured population by roughly 900,000 people as the provision phases in, a materially larger figure than earlier Kaiser Family Foundation estimates, reflecting different scoring assumptions about affected populations.

This is a national implementation date, not a proposal — providers with meaningful caseloads of refugees, asylees, or other affected noncitizen categories should expect enrollment attrition starting now, concentrated in states with larger refugee and asylee populations such as Washington, California, New York, Massachusetts, and Minnesota.
items.creditImplication: I would reassess payer-mix and census assumptions for personal care, home health, and HCBS borrowers with concentrated exposure to refugee, asylee, or humanitarian-parolee populations in high-immigrant states, since this is a real, dated enrollment loss rather than a future risk.

items.headline: Mississippi Begins Auto-Suspending Non-EVV Personal Care and Private Duty Nursing Claims
items.status: Implemented October 1, 2026; non-compliant claims are now auto-suspended.
items.bodyHtml:
As of October 1, 2026, Mississippi Medicaid requires that all State Plan Private Duty Nursing (PDN) and Personal Care Services (PCS) claims be submitted and processed through the Electronic Visit Verification (EVV) system via its aggregator, HHAeXchange. The state's MESA claims system now automatically suspends any fee-for-service PDN or PCS claim that does not originate from HHAeXchange, enforcing the federal 21st Century Cures Act EVV mandate that other states have already implemented for personal care.

Mississippi is offering a temporary exception process for providers experiencing ongoing technical onboarding issues, allowing continued direct MESA billing while issues are resolved, but only with prior state approval — unapproved direct submissions after the deadline are denied and redirected to HHAeXchange.

This is a claims-processing enforcement change, not a rate change: it does not alter PDN or PCS reimbursement rates, but it directly affects whether claims get paid on time.
items.creditImplication: For Mississippi-based PDN and PCS borrowers, I want evidence of full HHAeXchange onboarding or an approved exception before underwriting near-term cash flow — claim suspensions from incomplete EVV integration are a real, immediate DSO and liquidity risk, not a theoretical one.

items.headline: Kansas Launches Community Supports Waiver, Capped at 500 Enrollees and $20,000 Per Person
items.status: Effective October 1, 2026, with launch announced October 3, 2026; CMS approved the 1915(c) waiver July 1, 2026.
items.bodyHtml:
Kansas has launched its new Community Supports Waiver, a 1915(c) HCBS waiver for residents age 5 and older with intellectual or developmental disabilities who do not require 24-hour paid support but would otherwise need placement in an Intermediate Care Facility for Individuals with Intellectual Disabilities (ICF/IID). CMS approved the waiver on July 1, 2026, and it became operative October 1, 2026, administered by the Kansas Department for Aging and Disability Services (KDADS) with the Kansas Department of Health and Environment, coordinating with existing KanCare managed care networks.

CMS approved a projected enrollment of 500 individuals for the first waiver year, running October 1, 2026 through September 30, 2027, with services subject to an annual cap of $20,000 per participant. Covered services include personal care, respite, employment supports, assistive technology, home modifications, and non-medical transportation; day and residential services are excluded. The state's stated purpose is to reduce its I/DD waiver waiting list.

Both the enrollment cap and the per-person dollar cap are binding constraints, not targets — this is a modest, deliberately bounded expansion rather than an open-ended new funding stream.
items.creditImplication: I would treat this as a small, capped incremental revenue opportunity for Kansas I/DD and HCBS providers — useful for waitlist-driven referral volume, but the 500-enrollee and $20,000-per-person caps mean it cannot support aggressive growth projections for any single operator.

sources.label: Office of the Governor of Kansas

items.headline: Federal Court Vacates Community-Integration Provisions of HHS Section 504 Rule
items.status: Order and Final Judgment entered September 23, 2026, in Texas v. Kennedy (N.D. Tex., Lubbock Div., No. 5:24-CV-225-H); not a rulemaking and not subject to a comment period.
items.bodyHtml:
On September 23, 2026, the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Texas entered an Order and Final Judgment in Texas v. Kennedy, granting a joint motion by the Department of Justice (on behalf of HHS) and the states of Texas, Florida, Alaska, Louisiana, and Montana. The order vacates the 'most integrated setting' definition and the entire community-integration provision of HHS's 2024 Section 504 regulation, including its application to existing facilities, education programs, and medical diagnostic equipment.

Importantly, the order does not change the underlying Section 504 statute or Title II of the ADA, does not overturn the Supreme Court's Olmstead decision requiring integrated settings where appropriate, and does not touch CMS's separate HCBS settings rule governing where Medicaid HCBS services may be delivered. What it removes is a specific HHS regulatory mechanism that civil-rights and disability advocates had used to press federal agencies and states toward community-based rather than institutional placement.

The practical effect on day-to-day HCBS waiver administration is not yet clear — this was a negotiated resolution between DOJ and the plaintiff states rather than a new policy directive to states, and no state has yet announced a resulting change to waiver enrollment, waitlist management, or institutional-placement practices as a direct result.
items.creditImplication: I would not read this as a near-term change to HCBS funding or waiver enrollment, but it removes one federal enforcement lever that has supported HCBS expansion over institutional care — worth tracking for second-order effects on state waiver pipelines rather than acting on now.

items.headline: CY2027 Home Health Payment Rule Remains Proposed, Not Final
items.status: Proposed July 1, 2026; comment period closed August 31, 2026; no final rule issued as of this week.
items.bodyHtml:
CMS's Calendar Year 2027 Home Health Prospective Payment System proposed rule, published July 1, 2026, would deliver a net 2.4% aggregate payment increase (about $420 million) relative to CY2026 — combining the statutory 2.1% annual update with a 0.3% increase tied to the outlier fixed-dollar-loss ratio. Notably, this is the first year since CY2022 that CMS has not proposed an additional permanent negative adjustment on top of the statutory update.

However, the proposal would also continue a temporary -3.0% reduction to the national standardized 30-day payment rate, intended to recoup an estimated $500 million in prior Patient-Driven Groupings Model (PDGM) overpayments. That temporary cut already applies under current CY2026 rates and is not new; the proposal is to extend it into CY2027 rather than let it expire.

The comment period closed August 31, 2026, and CMS has not yet issued a final rule; it typically finalizes the Home Health PPS rule in early November for a January 1 effective date, so a final rule is expected but not yet in hand.

Until finalized, neither the headline 2.4% increase nor the continuation of the -3.0% adjustment is locked in — CMS could adjust either figure in the final rule.
items.creditImplication: I would continue underwriting home health borrowers on current CY2026 rates, including the existing -3.0% PDGM recoupment adjustment that is already in effect, and would not build the proposed 2.4% CY2027 increase into forward cash-flow projections until a final rule is published.

focusHtml: The diligence items I'd prioritize this week: for personal care, HCBS, and home health borrowers in Washington, California, New York, Massachusetts, and Minnesota, pull current payer-mix detail to quantify exposure to refugee, asylee, and other now-restricted noncitizen categories ahead of further enrollment attrition. For any Mississippi-based PDN or PCS operator, confirm actual HHAeXchange EVV onboarding status or an approved exception letter — not just an attestation of intent — since non-compliant claims are being suspended now. For Kansas I/DD or HCBS operators citing the new Community Supports Waiver as a growth driver, size their revenue assumptions against the hard 500-enrollee and $20,000-per-participant caps rather than the headline program launch. More broadly, continue treating the CY2027 Home Health PPS proposed rule as unconfirmed in any cash-flow model, and revisit EVV compliance history, provider revalidation status, and denied-claim trends across all HCBS and personal-care credits given the pattern of states (Mississippi this week, Minnesota's ongoing 80% EVV compliance enforcement) tightening claims-level program integrity enforcement rather than changing rates.

title: Weekly Medicaid, Home Health & HCBS Update
overviewHtml: This was a quiet week for actual reimbursement changes but an active one for the administrative machinery that will determine how much cash flows to home care, HCBS and skilled providers over the next year. The dominant theme is state-level and advisory-body activity around policies enacted or proposed earlier in 2026: states are diverging in how strictly they will enforce Medicaid work-requirement medical-frailty exemptions ahead of the January 1, 2027 federal deadline, and MACPAC used its September 24-25 public meeting to formally weigh in on two still-pending CMS rules that would cap state directed payments and tighten provider-tax financing, both of which fund Medicaid managed-care rates that support LTSS and HCBS providers. Separately, the nationwide home health and hospice enrollment moratorium remains in effect with no CMS decision yet on whether it will lift as scheduled on November 13, 2026. I want to be explicit about what did NOT happen: there was no new Medicare home health payment cut this week — the CY2027 proposed rule on the table would actually raise aggregate payments 2.4%, and it has not been finalized; no Medicaid work requirement is actually in effect anywhere yet outside early-adopter states: the national mandate does not bind until January 1, 2027; and CMS has not announced any extension, modification or lifting of the home health/hospice enrollment moratorium this week — it is simply still pending.

items.headline: States split on documentation vs. self-attestation for Medicaid work-requirement medical-frailty exemptions
items.status: Administrative choice being made now by states ahead of the federal January 1, 2027 work-requirement effective date; not yet a binding national requirement.
items.bodyHtml:
CMS's interim final rule implementing the One Big Beautiful Bill Act's Medicaid community engagement (work) requirement allows states to accept a beneficiary's self-attestation of a medically frail or disabling condition for the first enrollment cycle, with documentation required at least every 12 months starting in 2028. Reporting this week (AP, September 26) found at least six states — Arkansas, Idaho, Indiana, New Hampshire, North Carolina and Ohio — plan to require documentation immediately rather than accept self-attestation, going further than the federal floor requires.

The underlying mandate applies to roughly 20 million expansion-population adults across the 41 expansion states plus D.C. and does not take effect until January 1, 2027 (states may move earlier via 1115 authority). CBO projects $887 billion in federal savings and 7.5 million fewer insured over the decade tied to the broader reconciliation law, of which work requirements are one component; Arizona has already seen a 55% Medicaid enrollment drop (over 400,000 beneficiaries) since April 2025 tied to related administrative friction, illustrating the churn risk even before the mandate is formally binding nationwide.

Most direct-care Medicaid HCBS and personal care beneficiaries qualify through aged/disabled eligibility pathways that are exempt from the work requirement itself, but the medically frail exemption process matters because it is the mechanism by which beneficiaries who are nominally in the expansion group but functionally disabled avoid disenrollment. States requiring upfront clinical documentation create a higher administrative burden that can produce coverage gaps for borderline cases before January 2027.
items.creditImplication: I am not yet underwriting to any revenue impact from work requirements since the mandate is not in effect anywhere on a mandatory basis, but I am flagging the six stricter-documentation states as higher near-term churn risk for payer mix and private-pay conversion once the rule binds in 2027, and I want borrowers in those states to show a plan for exemption-verification support for frail clients.

sources.label: CMS – Medicaid Community Engagement Requirement Interim Final Rule Fact Sheet
AP via US News – As work requirements kick in for Medicaid, some states are taking a tougher stance

items.headline: MACPAC reviews pending caps on Medicaid state directed payments and provider-tax financing
items.status: Advisory review only; underlying CMS proposed rules had comments close July 21, 2026 and are not yet finalized.
items.bodyHtml:
At its September 24-25, 2026 public meeting, the Medicaid and CHIP Payment and Access Commission (MACPAC) formally reviewed two CMS proposed rules issued under Section 71116 of the 2025 reconciliation law: one capping Medicaid managed-care state directed payments (SDPs) and certain fee-for-service targeted practitioner payments at 100% of Medicare rates in expansion states (110% in non-expansion states), and a companion proposal narrowing the health care-related (provider) tax hold-harmless test. CMS estimates the SDP rule alone at roughly $775 billion in total savings and $510 billion in federal savings over ten years; the comment period on both rules closed July 21, 2026, and neither has been finalized.

MACPAC's commissioners, in a comment letter to CMS Administrator Dr. Mehmet Oz, warned that applying the Medicare-based limits at the service level could constrain states' ability to use SDPs to support access and quality goals, and that combining the new taxable-provider class with elimination of the so-called 75/75 test removes a pathway states use to raise Medicaid revenue with only a loose tie to program spending. SDPs are a significant funding lever in Medicaid managed long-term services and supports (MLTSS) states, where they are used to raise managed-care rates paid through to home health, personal care and HCBS network providers.

Neither rule is in effect. This week's development is MACPAC's formal advisory input, not a new CMS action, but it signals where a future final rule is likely to land and which provider types (rate-dependent MLTSS networks) are most exposed if the caps are finalized largely as proposed.
items.creditImplication: Where a borrower's state relies on state directed payments to prop up Medicaid MCO rates for HCBS or personal care, I am treating any embedded rate assumptions in projections as at risk pending finalization of this rule, and I am not underwriting to current SDP-supported rate levels as permanent until CMS issues a final rule and states show how they will respond.

sources.label: MACPAC – State Directed Payment and Provider Tax Proposed Rule (September 2026 meeting)
CMS – CMS Moves to Rein In Misused Medicaid Dollars and Reward Quality Care

items.headline: Nationwide home health and hospice enrollment moratorium remains in effect; no CMS decision yet on November expiration
items.status: In effect since May 13, 2026; six-month term runs through November 13, 2026, and CMS has not announced whether it will extend, modify or let it lapse.
items.bodyHtml:
CMS's nationwide moratorium on new Medicare enrollment of home health agencies and hospices, announced under the administration's anti-fraud task force, took effect May 13, 2026 and blocks new HHA/hospice enrollments and certain majority-ownership changes requiring re-enrollment; currently enrolled providers are unaffected and may continue normal operations. The moratorium runs for a fixed six-month term and CMS must decide before it lapses whether to let it expire, extend it, or replace it with a different enforcement approach, with any extension required to be announced in the Federal Register.

Industry groups, including LeadingAge and the National Alliance for Care at Home, have pressed CMS to let the moratorium expire on schedule rather than renew it, arguing that fraud is concentrated in specific metro markets rather than distributed nationally, and citing data that 38% of Medicare beneficiaries referred to home health after a hospital discharge in Q3 2025 did not receive those services — an access argument against extending a blanket new-enrollment freeze. As of this week, CMS has made no public announcement on its intentions.

This is a live, unresolved variable rather than new news this week, but it remains squarely relevant to underwriting because it directly freezes de novo entry and constrains change-of-ownership structuring for the sector through at least mid-November.
items.creditImplication: For any deal involving a new HHA/hospice start-up or a change of ownership that would trigger Medicare re-enrollment, I am treating Medicare billing capability as frozen until CMS's decision lands, and I am building the November 13 decision date into closing and funding timelines for any pending home health or hospice M&A.

sources.label: CMS – Home Health and Hospice Nationwide Moratorium Q&As
Home Health Care News – As Home Health Moratorium Nears Expiration, Advocates Press CMS Against Extension

items.headline: CY2027 Medicare home health proposed rule would raise payments 2.4%, not cut them — but is not yet final
items.status: Proposed rule only; public comment period closed August 31, 2026; CMS has not issued a final rule.
items.bodyHtml:
CMS's CY2027 Home Health Prospective Payment System proposed rule (CMS-1844-P), issued July 1, 2026, would increase aggregate Medicare payments to home health agencies by an estimated 2.4%, or $420 million, relative to CY2026 — a reversal from CY2026's finalized 1.3% ($220 million) aggregate cut and from CY2026's own proposed rule, which had floated a 6.4% reduction before finalization. This is a proposal only; CMS has not yet published a final rule, and none of the CY2027 figures are in effect.

The proposed rule also carries forward a temporary 3.0% reduction to the national standardized 30-day payment rate, which CMS characterizes as recouping prior-year overpayments tied to the PDGM case-mix transition. Industry commenters, including the National Alliance for Care at Home, argue that permanent PDGM-related reductions have already cut the 30-day payment rate by 9.37% cumulatively and that a single positive headline update does not offset years of recoupment. The comment period closed August 31, 2026 with 657 comments submitted, a far smaller volume than the 952,483 comments received on the prior year's rule.

CMS typically finalizes the annual HH PPS rule around November 1 for a January 1 effective date, so a final CY2027 rule is likely within the next several weeks but had not been issued as of this week.
items.creditImplication: I am not building the proposed 2.4% increase into any CY2027 projections until CMS finalizes the rule, and I am specifically flagging the contested 3% behavioral recoupment adjustment as a real downside risk to modeled cash flow for Medicare-heavy home health borrowers even if the headline number is finalized as an increase.

sources.label: CMS – CY2027 Home Health PPS Proposed Rule Fact Sheet (CMS-1844-P)
Home Health Care News – What Comments Reveal About CMS' Proposed Medicare Home Health Rule

focusHtml: The diligence priorities this week are financing-mechanism exposure rather than immediate rate cuts: for any Medicaid managed-care-heavy HCBS or personal care borrower, I want a state-by-state breakdown of how much of the payer rate rides on state directed payments or provider-tax-funded supplemental payments, since both are subject to pending federal caps reviewed by MACPAC this week. For home health and hospice operators, I want current Medicare enrollment status confirmed and any planned change-of-ownership transaction stress-tested against the moratorium's November 13 decision date, since a CHOW requiring re-enrollment cannot close through Medicare in the interim. For multi-state operators, I want to know which states are already requiring upfront documentation for work-requirement medical-frailty exemptions, since that is the earliest observable signal of how aggressively a state will administer the January 2027 mandate. And across the board, I am continuing to track Medicaid DSO, denied-claim trends, EVV compliance and revalidation status as baseline diligence items — none of which moved this week, but all of which become more consequential once the financing and enrollment questions above are resolved.

title: Weekly Medicaid, Home Health & HCBS Update
overviewHtml: This was a comparatively quiet week for federal Medicaid and home health rulemaking, but it produced one significant piece of consolidation news and one state-level payment story that illustrate the two forces underwriters are juggling right now: continued fraud-driven friction on the enrollment and payment side, and pockets of real rate relief in states that had frozen Medicaid rates for years. Addus HomeCare's agreement to buy AccentCare's personal care division for roughly $275 million was the week's dominant transaction, and California's move to end a multi-year freeze on pediatric private-duty nursing rates was the week's dominant payment story, though that increase is not effective until January 1, 2027. I want to be explicit about what did not happen: there was no new federal Medicare home health payment cut this week, no government shutdown at the September 30 fiscal-year-end (Congress passed a continuing resolution on September 2 funding the government through December 11, 2026), and no announced extension or narrowing of the nationwide home health/hospice Medicare enrollment moratorium, which remains in effect on the terms CMS set in May.

items.headline: Addus HomeCare to acquire AccentCare's personal care division for $275 million
items.status: Definitive agreement signed September 14, 2026; deal not yet closed, pending regulatory approvals and customary closing conditions.
items.bodyHtml:
Addus HomeCare Corporation announced a definitive agreement on September 14, 2026 to acquire AccentCare's personal care division, excluding AccentCare's New York operations, for approximately $275 million. AccentCare retains its home health and hospice lines outside this transaction. The acquired operations serve an average daily census of approximately 13,700 clients across 10 states and are expected to add roughly $280 million in annualized revenue, about a 19% increase to Addus' current revenue base.

The deal deepens Addus' existing footprint in Texas, Illinois, California and Arizona and adds new-state entry into Colorado, Georgia, Minnesota, Pennsylvania, Tennessee and Washington. Per Addus' Form 8-K, the company will fund the purchase through a combination of its revolver and cash on hand, and the filing states the transaction is expected to close following completion of regulatory approvals and customary closing conditions; neither the 8-K nor the company's public statements specify an exact closing date. This follows Addus' Gentiva personal care acquisition and its May 2026 HomeCourt deal in Indiana, continuing a pattern of programmatic personal-care consolidation.

Because the transaction covers personal care (a largely Medicaid-funded, non-clinical service line) rather than Medicare-certified home health or hospice, it falls outside the nationwide home health/hospice Medicare enrollment moratorium CMS put in place in May 2026, but the deal will still require state-level Medicaid change-of-ownership approvals in each of the 10 states involved before it can fund and integrate.
items.creditImplication: I read this as a leveraged-but-manageable draw on Addus' balance sheet (revolver plus cash, no new debt disclosed) and a signal that personal-care multiples remain attractive to consolidators even amid fraud-enforcement headwinds; for AccentCare and other multi-line operators, it confirms that divesting personal care to fund core home health/hospice investment is a live playbook I should watch for at other national platforms.

items.headline: California ends multi-year freeze on pediatric private-duty nursing Medicaid rates
items.status: Enacted as part of California's FY2026-27 budget; the rate increase itself does not take effect until January 1, 2027.
items.bodyHtml:
California's enacted 2026-27 state budget includes a rate increase for pediatric private-duty nursing (PDN) services paid through Medi-Cal, ending what providers describe as an eight-to-nine-year rate freeze. The increase is scheduled to take effect January 1, 2027, not immediately. California pays for PDN directly through fee-for-service Medicaid rather than through managed care organizations, which is why this is a direct state rate action rather than a plan-level negotiation.

Aveanna Healthcare, the largest pediatric PDN provider affected, cited the change as a factor in raising its full-year 2026 guidance and said it expects the rate increase to help reverse years of caregiver-wage-driven capacity constraints in the state, with plans to raise caregiver wages ahead of the January 1 effective date and ramp recruiting once the higher rate is in place.

I could not verify an exact percentage or per-hour dollar figure for the new rate from primary sources; trade coverage describes the change only as a 'significant investment' without CMS or DHCS having published the specific rate schedule as of this week. Readers should treat any specific percentage figure circulating in secondary press as unconfirmed until DHCS publishes the implementing rate letter.
items.creditImplication: This is a real, budgeted rate improvement, but it is not yet cash-flowing, it does not take effect until January 1, 2027, and California could still delay or trim it in the interim budget process; I would not upgrade a California-concentrated PDN credit's underwritten rate assumptions until the DHCS rate letter is published and the increase is actually being paid.

items.headline: Nationwide Medicare enrollment moratorium on home health agencies and hospices remains in force, set to expire November 13, 2026
items.status: Implemented since May 13, 2026; still active this week, with no extension or modification announced.
items.bodyHtml:
CMS's nationwide, six-month moratorium on new Medicare enrollments for home health agencies and hospices took effect May 13, 2026 and, absent an extension, is scheduled to lapse November 13, 2026. The moratorium blocks CMS from processing new HHA and hospice Medicare enrollment applications and also restricts certain majority-ownership changes that would otherwise require Medicare re-enrollment; currently enrolled, Medicare-certified providers are unaffected and may continue normal operations. CMS has authority to extend the moratorium in additional six-month increments but has not announced an extension as of this week.

The action was taken under CMS's Vice President-led Anti-Fraud Task Force initiative and sits alongside other 2026 program-integrity measures, including a separate six-month DMEPOS enrollment moratorium that expired August 27, 2026, and the CMS Medicaid Fraud War Room, which CMS said had stopped more than $203 million in Medicaid payments to high-risk providers in its first 88 days of operation.

Accreditation and compliance bodies (ACHC, CHAP) have published FAQ guidance clarifying which ownership transactions qualify as exempt from re-enrollment, but the precise boundary of 'certain majority ownership changes' subject to the freeze is not fully codified in the Federal Register notice and is being worked out case-by-case with CMS regional offices.
items.creditImplication: For any home health or hospice acquisition structured as a change of majority ownership requiring Medicare re-enrollment, I need to confirm with counsel and CMS whether the specific transaction structure is exempt before assuming a clean close before November 13; de novo Medicare-certified entry is effectively frozen nationwide until the moratorium lapses or is extended, which supports valuations for existing certified licenses as scarce assets.

items.headline: No FY2027 government shutdown; funding extended through December 11, 2026
items.status: Enacted; continuing resolution signed into law September 2, 2026, funding federal agencies at FY2026 levels through December 11, 2026.
items.bodyHtml:
Congress passed and President Trump signed a continuing resolution on September 2, 2026, funding federal agencies, including CMS and HHS, at FY2026 levels through December 11, 2026. This removed the risk of a funding lapse at the October 1 start of FY2027, which had been a live concern through the summer. None of the twelve annual appropriations bills for FY2027 have been enacted, so the same funding-cliff risk resurfaces in mid-December, now positioned closer to, rather than colliding with, the November midterm elections.

During past shutdowns, CMS has generally been able to sustain Medicaid and Medicare benefit payments in the near term because Medicaid has multi-quarter advance funding and Medicare runs on a 14-day payment floor, but administrative functions such as new state plan amendment and waiver approvals typically stall. None of that materialized this week because no lapse occurred.
items.creditImplication: I am flagging this mainly as a negative-space item: readers should not assume any payment disruption, waiver-approval delay, or claims-processing slowdown occurred this week on account of a shutdown, because none took place; the December 11 deadline is the next date to calendar for potential administrative-approval risk on pending state waiver and SPA submissions.

sources.label: Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget - Appropriations Watch

focusHtml: For credits with California PDN or personal-care exposure, I would confirm current payer mix and whether the borrower is a fee-for-service Medi-Cal biller (as PDN is) versus managed care, and hold off crediting any pro forma benefit from the rate increase until DHCS publishes the implementing rate letter ahead of the January 1, 2027 effective date. For any home health or hospice borrower contemplating a sale or recapitalization before November 13, 2026, I would get specific confirmation — not an assumption — on whether the deal structure counts as a 'majority ownership change requiring re-enrollment' under the CMS moratorium, since that determines whether the transaction can close as planned or needs to be sequenced around the moratorium's lapse or extension. For personal-care platforms, the Addus/AccentCare deal is a useful multiple and structure comp; I'd want each state's Medicaid change-of-ownership approval timeline mapped separately, since that — not the federal moratorium — is the binding constraint on this particular transaction. More broadly, this week's quiet on new federal rate cuts is a reminder to keep tracking denied-claim trends, provider revalidation status, and EVV compliance directly with each borrower rather than assuming stability from an absence of headlines.

title: Weekly Medicaid, Home Health & HCBS Update
overviewHtml: The dominant theme this week is intensifying federal program-integrity enforcement across home health, hospice, and durable medical equipment — not a new reimbursement cut. The nationwide Medicare enrollment moratorium on home health agencies and hospices, in place since mid-May, drew sharper industry pushback this week after the National Alliance for Care at Home publicly urged CMS to narrow it, arguing it is freezing legitimate de novo expansion and provider affiliations rather than only rooting out fraud; CMS made no decision this week to extend, narrow, or lift it. Separately, CMS barred eleven durable medical equipment suppliers tied to over $3.4 billion in suspected fraudulent billing, and Georgia's hard EVV enforcement deadline for home health claims arrives September 14. I want to be explicit about what did NOT happen this week: there was no new federal Medicare or Medicaid rate cut to home health, hospice, or HCBS providers, the CY 2027 Home Health proposed rule (a net 2.4% aggregate increase) is unchanged and still pending finalization, the proposed Medicaid provider-tax restrictions remain just a proposal with comments due September 21, and California's roughly $1.7 billion in deferred IHSS-related Medicaid payments remains an unresolved, ongoing liquidity question rather than a new development.

items.headline: Nationwide Medicare enrollment moratorium on home health agencies and hospices continues; industry group escalates pushback
items.status: In effect since May 13, 2026 for an initial six-month term running through mid-November 2026; CMS took no action this week to extend, narrow, or lift it.
items.bodyHtml:
CMS's nationwide moratorium, announced in a Federal Register notice effective May 13, 2026, bars new Medicare enrollment of home health agencies and hospices and blocks certain majority ownership changes that would otherwise require re-enrollment. Already-enrolled, Medicare-certified providers are unaffected and continue billing normally, and applications filed before the effective date may continue processing. CMS has authority to renew the moratorium in additional six-month increments if it determines fraud concerns persist, or to lift it early.

On September 9, the National Alliance for Care at Home publicly renewed its call for CMS to replace the blanket freeze with a targeted, risk-based approach. The Alliance said long-standing, high-quality hospices and home health agencies that have been approached by underserved communities to extend services are unable to do so solely because of the moratorium, and that it is also blocking hospice and home health agency affiliations with health systems, leaving financially stressed providers unable to be acquired and at greater risk of closure. This is industry advocacy rather than new CMS data, and CMS has not indicated any change in position.

Nothing about the moratorium's scope or duration changed this week — it remains a temporary, time-limited enrollment freeze, not a permanent barrier to entry, and it does not affect existing providers' ability to bill or operate.
items.creditImplication: I treat any deal premised on de novo Medicare enrollment or a majority-ownership change-of-control in home health or hospice as effectively frozen until the moratorium lifts; new platform builds in this space should be structured around acquiring an already-enrolled, active CCN rather than new enrollment. I'm watching for CMS's decision near mid-November on whether to extend, narrow, or let the moratorium lapse, since that will determine how long these deal-structuring constraints persist.

items.headline: CMS proposed rule restricting Medicaid provider taxes remains just a proposal; comments due September 21
items.status: Proposed rule, not final. Comment period closes September 21, 2026.
items.bodyHtml:
CMS issued a proposed rule on July 21, 2026 implementing two of H.R. 1's restrictions on how states use provider taxes to help finance the state share of Medicaid spending. The proposal would eliminate the alternative '75/75' indirect hold-harmless test, leaving a new class-specific threshold as the sole safe harbor, and would phase down the hold-harmless threshold for Medicaid expansion states from 5.5% to 3.5%; nursing facility and intermediate-care facility classes are exempted from that phasedown. States with a CMS-approved threshold above 6% under the prior test as of July 4, 2025 would be permitted to retain it, subject to the statutory phasedown.

CMS actuaries estimate the proposal would reduce federal Medicaid spending by approximately $246 billion over ten years nationwide. The rule proposes an October 1, 2026 effective date for eliminating the 75/75 test, but that date depends on CMS finalizing the rule almost immediately after the September 21 comment deadline — a tight turnaround that has not happened yet and is not guaranteed.

This rule does not set home health, HCBS, or personal care rates directly; it governs the financing mechanism many states use to fund the non-federal share of Medicaid, including HCBS and personal care rate add-ons. Nothing in this rule has taken effect, and no state's Medicaid rates have changed as a result of it this week.
items.creditImplication: I am not adjusting any rate assumptions off this rule since it is still proposed and unfinalized. Where a borrower operates in states that rely heavily on provider taxes to fund Medicaid HCBS or personal care rates, I want to know how state budget offices are contingency-planning for this rule in FY2027 forecasts, since a final rule finalized on any timeline would flow through state financing well before it reaches provider rates.

items.headline: Georgia's hard EVV enforcement deadline for home health claims arrives September 14
items.status: Takes effect September 14, 2026 for claims with that date of service or later; a voluntary 'soft go-live' has been running since August 31, 2026.
items.bodyHtml:
Under Georgia Medicaid's electronic visit verification program, all applicable Home Health Care Services (HHCS) claims — covering home health aide, skilled nursing, and physical, occupational, and speech therapy visits — with dates of service on or after September 14, 2026 must be submitted through the EVV system. This is part of the federal 21st Century Cures Act EVV mandate, which is now fully operational nationwide for both personal care services and home health care services claims.

States including Georgia enforce EVV compliance through automated 'hard edits' — validation rules that reject non-compliant claims before payment, with no warning period or grace window once the enforcement date passes. Providers have had a soft go-live period since August 31, 2026 to register, test, and become familiar with the system before mandatory enforcement begins.

This is a state-level operational deadline, not a new federal rule; other states have staggered EVV hard-enforcement dates of their own, and CMS is separately reviewing how states use EVV data for Medicaid program-integrity purposes nationally.
items.creditImplication: For any borrower with Georgia home health or PCS volume, I want to see EVV integration testing results and visit-capture compliance rates ahead of September 14, and I would stress-test days sales outstanding for a claim-rejection spike in the weeks immediately following go-live, consistent with what has occurred in other states after hard-edit rollouts.

items.headline: CMS bars 11 DME suppliers tied to $3.4 billion in suspected fraud, expanding use of the Medicare Advantage Preclusion List
items.status: Implemented September 8, 2026 — 11 suppliers added to the CMS Preclusion List, barring Medicare Advantage Part C/D payment.
items.bodyHtml:
CMS announced on September 8, 2026 that it identified and barred 11 durable medical equipment, prosthetics, orthotics, and supplies (DMEPOS) suppliers, tied to more than $3.4 billion in suspected fraudulent billing across 2025 and 2026, from receiving future Medicare Advantage Part C and Part D payments. None of the 11 suppliers had submitted claims prior to 2025, and CMS cited practices including billing for equipment supplied to beneficiaries who had already died and equipment beneficiaries never requested or received. Four of the suppliers had previously been revoked from Original Medicare and had shifted to billing Medicare Advantage plans instead.

All 11 companies were added to the CMS Preclusion List, which blocks payment for Medicare Part D drugs and Medicare Advantage services or items they prescribe or furnish.

This action targets DMEPOS suppliers, not home health, hospice, or HCBS agencies directly, and I am flagging it precisely so it is not mistaken for a home health enforcement action. It is relevant here as further evidence of the same anti-fraud enforcement push that produced the home health and hospice enrollment moratorium — CMS is broadening its use of enrollment revocation and preclusion tools across post-acute-adjacent provider types this quarter.
items.creditImplication: Where a borrower has an affiliated or subsidiary DME/DMEPOS billing line, or shared ownership with entities that have faced Medicare enrollment scrutiny, I want confirmation that none of those entities appear on the CMS Preclusion List and a description of the borrower's exclusion-screening protocol; this is a reminder to widen program-integrity diligence beyond the core home health/HCBS license when ownership structures span multiple provider types.

sources.label: CMS — CMS Cracks Down on Massive $3.4 Billion Medical Equipment Supplier Fraud Scheme

focusHtml: Given this week's developments, I'd prioritize four diligence threads. First, for any home health or hospice target, confirm the deal is structured as an acquisition of an already-enrolled, active CCN rather than a new Medicare enrollment or a majority-ownership change that could trip the nationwide moratorium, and check whether the target's growth plan assumed de novo licensure that is currently frozen. Second, for Georgia-exposed home health and PCS operators, get current EVV integration and visit-capture compliance data ahead of the September 14 hard-enforcement date, and more broadly map state-by-state EVV enforcement dates against the borrower's footprint, since denied-claim spikes tend to cluster around go-live. Third, where ownership structures include DME/DMEPOS billing alongside home health or HCBS lines, confirm none of the affiliated entities appear on the CMS Preclusion List and review the exclusion-screening protocol, given CMS's expanding use of enrollment revocation this quarter. Fourth, for California-exposed IHSS or personal care borrowers, track the roughly $1.7 billion in deferred federal Medicaid payments as an open state Medicaid DSO and working-capital risk — it remains a deferral pending documentation review rather than a rate cut, but it has been unresolved for months and warrants a standing diligence question on state payment timing and any state-level bridge funding.
